summary: Gives an overview of ways to tunnel IPv6 over IPv4 networks, including those in current use, some now historic and some newer and uncommon. It aims to help people with an IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling need select suitable mechanisms.

eli5.summary: A comparison of different ways to smuggle new-style letters through old-style roads.

questions: which ipv6 tunnel should i use
subtitle: Comparing methods to carry IPv6 traffic over IPv4 networks

tldr.problem: During the transition from IPv4 to IPv6, networks may have IPv6-only islands separated by IPv4-only infrastructure, requiring a way to bridge these networks.
tldr.mechanism: Multiple tunnel mechanisms exist, each encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets with different trade-offs in simplicity, deployment, security, and reliability.
tldr.outcome: Different environments favor different mechanisms: configured tunnels work well for point-to-point links with predictable performance, while public gateway mechanisms like 6to4 and Teredo support broader deployment but with less control and more variability.

facts.value: Used by configured tunnels, automatic tunneling, 6over4, 6to4, ISATAP, 6rd

today: RFC 7059 remains an Informational document describing the tunnel landscape as of 2013. It is not a standard and does not specify any mechanisms itself. The mechanisms it surveys remain in use: configured tunnels continue to be the most reliable option for point-to-point links, 6rd is deployed by some ISPs, and mechanisms like Teredo and 6bed4 serve specialized use cases. 6to4's problems with public relays are well-documented, and native IPv6 deployment has reduced the need for tunneling in many networks.

sections.title: Overview of IPv6-over-IPv4 Tunneling
sections.content:
As the Internet transitions from IPv4 to IPv6, networks often consist of IPv6-capable islands separated by IPv4-only infrastructure. Tunneling solves this by encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets, allowing IPv6 traffic to traverse IPv4 networks unchanged. This document surveys the landscape of tunnel mechanisms available, ranging from the simple and widely deployed to the specialized and novel.

The mechanisms discussed include manually configured tunnels, automatic tunneling, 6to4 relays, Teredo (which works through NAT), and several others developed for specific use cases like ISP last-mile deployment or peer-to-peer networks. Each mechanism represents a different point in a design space defined by simplicity, overhead, deployment model, NAT compatibility, and reliability.
sections.eli5: When you need to send IPv6 letters but the roads only understand IPv4, you put the IPv6 letter inside an IPv4 envelope and send it.

sections.title: Key Tunneling Concepts
sections.content:
All tunnel mechanisms share the fundamental principle of encapsulation: wrapping an IPv6 packet as the payload of an IPv4 packet. The outer IPv4 header carries protocol number 41 (or a wrapper protocol like UDP) to indicate that IPv6 data is inside. Some mechanisms like configured tunnels require manual setup of the remote tunnel endpoint address, while others derive it from the IPv6 address itself.

A critical distinction divides mechanisms into two categories: point-to-point tunnels, where a fixed remote endpoint is configured, and NBMA (Non-Broadcast Multi-Access) tunnels, where packets can reach multiple destinations through gateways or relays. Point-to-point tunnels offer predictable performance but require explicit configuration. NBMA mechanisms offer broader connectivity and easier deployment but introduce unpredictability and potential reliability issues.
sections.eli5: Some tunnels connect two specific places, like a tunnel under a river between two towns. Others are more like highways where many towns can connect through shared exits.

sections.title: Categories of Tunnel Mechanisms
sections.content:
Configured tunnels (sometimes called 6in4 or manual tunnels) are among the oldest and simplest mechanisms. They require explicit setup of the remote endpoint address but offer fully predictable behavior. These are widely implemented in operating systems and routers, making them suitable for connectivity between organizations or with tunnel brokers like tunnelbroker.net and SixXS.

6to4 and 6rd work automatically by embedding the IPv4 address inside the IPv6 address prefix, avoiding manual configuration. However, 6to4 relies on public anycast relays that may be unreliable or far away, causing performance issues. 6rd, by contrast, is designed for ISP deployment with provider-managed relays, offering better control. Other mechanisms like ISATAP (for enterprise networks), Teredo (for behind-NAT scenarios), and 6bed4 (for peer-to-peer) address specific deployment scenarios, each with distinct trade-offs between ease of use, NAT compatibility, and reliability.
sections.eli5: Some tunnels are like calling ahead to arrange a meeting at a specific place. Others figure out where to go from your address itself, like knowing which market to visit by your neighborhood.

sections.title: Deployment Decisions
sections.content:
Choosing a tunnel mechanism requires understanding the deployment context. Within a single organization's IPv4 network, ISATAP or 6over4 provide local IPv6 connectivity without relying on external infrastructure. For ISPs connecting subscribers, 6rd offers controlled deployment with provider-managed relays. For end-users needing global IPv6 connectivity without ISP support, configured tunnels through a tunnel broker provide stable performance, while 6to4 or Teredo offer automatic configuration at the cost of variable reliability.

NAT compatibility is critical for home and mobile users. Mechanisms using protocol 41 encapsulation do not work well through NAT, as NAT cannot multiplex multiple protocol 41 flows behind a single address. UDP-based mechanisms like Teredo, 6a44, AYIYA, and 6bed4 overcome this by using UDP port numbers for multiplexing, allowing multiple tunnel endpoints behind a single NAT. Performance, security, and operational simplicity further guide the choice in specific scenarios.
sections.eli5: If you control the network, you can set up a simple direct tunnel. If you're behind a family's shared Internet, you need a tunnel that uses port numbers so multiple tunnels can fit. If you want no configuration, you accept less reliable performance.

sections.title: Security Concerns and Modern Status
sections.content:
A key security concern with tunneling is that IPv6 connectivity may exist when network administrators did not intend it. Unmanaged tunnels can allow bypassing firewalls or access controls. Additionally, spoofed packets can easily enter tunnels without strong validation, potentially allowing attacks. The RFC emphasizes that ingress filtering and endpoint authentication must be explicitly applied—tunneling does not automatically provide security.

As of 2013 (the RFC's publication date), 6to4 has been largely disabled by default in operating systems due to reliability problems with public relays and issues with NAT prefix blocks. Configured tunnels remain the most robust mechanism for point-to-point links where configuration is acceptable. The landscape continues to evolve, with mechanisms like 6rd gaining traction for ISP deployments and Teredo serving niche use cases despite known limitations.
sections.eli5: A tunnel can let bad traffic slip through without anyone noticing. If you set up a tunnel, you're responsible for guarding it. Some automatic tunnels broke because shared relays didn't work reliably.
